objective: By the end of this lesson you can plan a VFR cross-country on a sectional chart, turn a true course into a compass heading, and fly it with a flight log by landmarks and pre-computed headings, times and groundspeeds.
why: GPS and radios can fail. A pilot who can read the ground, hold a heading and check the clock can always find the way and land with fuel to spare.

prereading.what: Charts, variation and deviation, wind effect, basic calculations, pilotage, dead reckoning, wind triangle and the Chickasha-to-Guthrie planning example.
prereading.label: PHAK Ch 16, 16-1 to 16-21

prereading.what: Magnetic compass: variation, deviation, turning and acceleration errors.
prereading.label: PHAK 8-23 to 8-27

prereading.printed: Chart Users' Guide, VFR Terms and Symbols pp 10-13
prereading.what: How terrain, obstructions and Maximum Elevation Figures are shown on a sectional.
prereading.label: Chart Guide Chart Users' Guide, VFR Terms and Symbols pp 10-13

warmup: Your GPS screen goes dark 20 minutes into a cross-country. What three things would you need to keep going to your destination?

key_terms.def: Navigating by looking at landmarks or checkpoints on the ground.
Navigating by math: time, airspeed, distance and direction, corrected for wind.
Your course line on the chart, measured clockwise from true north.
Angle between true north and magnetic north. Shown by isogonic lines on the chart.
Compass error caused by the airplane's own magnetic fields. Read it off the deviation card.
Degrees you point the nose into the wind so your track stays on course.
The actual path the airplane makes over the ground.
Speed over the ground: true airspeed adjusted for wind.
Calibrated airspeed corrected for altitude and nonstandard temperature. Used for flight planning.
Big blue number in each chart quadrant: highest terrain or obstacle there, in hundreds of feet MSL.

body.p: Pilotage means navigating by visible landmarks. Dead reckoning means computing direction and distance from a known position [[1:388|PHAK 16-1]].

head: Method
What you use
Best for
rows: Landmarks and checkpoints: roads, rivers, railroads, lakes, power lines [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]]
Time, airspeed, distance and direction, adjusted for wind, to get heading and GS [[1:400|PHAK 16-13]]
Holding a heading and timing each leg; over water it may be all you have

body.p: You use them together. Dead reckoning gives you a heading and a groundspeed. Pilotage checks them at each checkpoint, and you correct as needed [[1:400|PHAK 16-13]].
Know your chart scale. A sectional is 1:500,000, so 1 inch = 6.86 NM, or about 8 SM [[1:389|PHAK 16-2]]. Half an inch off the course line is about 3.43 NM on the ground [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].

callout.text: Beginning pilots should use radio navigation to back up pilotage, not replace it. That protects you if the radio fails [[1:409|PHAK 16-22]].

check.q: A checkpoint is half an inch from your course line on a sectional. About how far is that on the ground?

chunks.title: From true course to compass heading

body.p: Draw your course on the chart and measure it from a meridian near the middle of the course. That is the true course (TC) [[1:392|PHAK 16-5]]. Then fix it in this order:

callout.text: TC ± WCA = TH ± V = MH ± D = CH [[1:407|PHAK 16-20]]

head: Step
Rule
Where you get it
rows: Wind from the right: add. Wind from the left: subtract [[1:403|PHAK 16-16]]
West: add. East: subtract. "East is least, west is best" [[1:395|PHAK 16-8]]
Nearest isogonic line (dashed magenta) on the chart [[1:393|PHAK 16-6]]
Add or subtract as the card shows [[1:403|PHAK 16-16]]
Compass deviation card in the airplane

body.p: Variation is the same on any heading. Deviation changes with heading but not with location [[1:226|PHAK 8-24]]. Deviation comes from the airplane's electrical circuits, radios, lights, engine and magnetized parts [[1:395|PHAK 16-8]].
PHAK example, Chickasha to Guthrie: TC 031°, WCA 3° left gives TH 028°. Variation 7° E gives MH 021°. Deviation +2° gives compass heading 023° [[1:407|PHAK 16-20]].

callout.text: Card shows 0° at 180° and +2° at 210°? For 195°, use about +1°. You can interpolate in your head [[1:395|PHAK 16-8]].

check.q: In Los Angeles the variation is 14° E. What magnetic course do you fly for a true course of 180°?

chunks.title: Magnetic compass errors and turns to headings

body.p: The compass only reads right when its card is level, in steady flight [[1:228|PHAK 8-26]]. Beyond about 18° of bank its readings are erratic [[1:225|PHAK 8-23]].

head: Error
What you see
What to do
rows: Stop the turn before the heading: 15° + half your latitude [[1:228|PHAK 8-26]]
Let it pass the heading by the same amount before rolling out [[1:228|PHAK 8-26]]
Speed up: shows a turn to north. Slow down: shows a turn to south [[1:228|PHAK 8-26]]
Read it only at steady speed. Memory aid: ANDS [[1:228|PHAK 8-26]]
Use the average of the swings [[1:229|PHAK 8-27]]

body.p: Example: near 40° latitude, stop a turn to north 15 + 20 = 35° early. Near 30° latitude, stop a turn to south 15 + 15 = 30° past the heading [[1:228|PHAK 8-26]].

In practice, turn with the heading indicator and lead the rollout by about half your bank angle (30° bank, lead 15°) [[24:77|AFH 3-16]]. But the heading indicator drifts. Check it about every 15 minutes and reset it to the compass while straight and level at constant speed [[1:224|PHAK 8-22]].

callout.text: ANDS: Accelerate = North, Decelerate = South. Turning to north: stop early. Turning to south: go past.

check.q: You speed up on a heading of 090°. What does the compass show?

chunks.title: Reading the land: topography on the chart

body.p: Sectionals show terrain and obstacles five ways [[2:10|Chart Users' Guide p 10]]:

bullets: Contour lines join points of equal elevation, basic ones every 500 ft. Close lines mean steep slopes [[2:10|Chart Users' Guide p 10]].
Shaded relief shows how the terrain may look from the air, lit from the northwest [[2:10|Chart Users' Guide p 10]].
Color tints go from light green (low) to dark brown (high) [[2:11|Chart Users' Guide p 11]].
Obstruction symbols show man-made obstacles, usually those more than 200 ft AGL. The top is in MSL; AGL height is in parentheses [[2:11|Chart Users' Guide p 11]].
Maximum Elevation Figures (MEF) give the highest terrain or obstacle in each quadrant, rounded up to the next 100 ft [[2:12|Chart Users' Guide p 12]].

body.p: In this example the tower top is 2,649 ft MSL. Add 100 ft possible error to get 2,749, then round up: MEF 2,800 ft, printed as "28" [[2:12|Chart Users' Guide p 12]].

callout.text: Charts can be wrong or old. New roads and towers may not be on your chart yet [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]]. Guy wires are almost invisible, so never approach antennas closer than 500 ft above the tallest one [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]]. Wind turbine lights can be 200 to 300 ft below the blade tips [[2:11|Chart Users' Guide p 11]].

check.q: What does a blue "28" in a sectional quadrant tell you?
check.a: The highest terrain or obstacle in that quadrant is at most 2,800 ft MSL (MEF) [[2:12|Chart Users' Guide p 12]].

body.p: Check the weather first to see if the flight is possible and which route is best [[1:404|PHAK 16-17]].

**Route.** Draw the line from the center of the departure airport to the center of the destination. A non-direct route, such as one past a VOR, uses two or more straight legs [[1:405|PHAK 16-18]]. Check the line and both sides of it for airspace and rugged terrain [[1:405|PHAK 16-18]].

**Checkpoints.** Pick big, easy features: large towns (yellow on the chart), large lakes and rivers, or towns with an airport, highways and railroads. Skip towns shown as a small circle; they may be just a few houses [[1:405|PHAK 16-18]]. Use roads, rivers or railroads on each side of the course as brackets, and pick plenty of checkpoints [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].
**Altitude.** Find the highest terrain and the tallest obstacle on the route [[1:405|PHAK 16-18]]. Then apply the rules:

head: Rule
What it says
rows: More than 3,000 ft above the surface, below 18,000 MSL: magnetic course 0°-179° = odd thousands + 500 (3,500, 5,500); 180°-359° = even thousands + 500 (4,500, 6,500) [[60:467|14 CFR 91.159]] [[60:468|91.159(a)(2)]]
Congested areas: 1,000 ft above the highest obstacle within 2,000 ft. Elsewhere: 500 ft above the surface. Anywhere: high enough to land safely if the engine quits [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119]]
Not less than 500 ft above the tallest one [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]]

body.p: In the PHAK example the pilot chose 5,500 ft MSL: above the Class C and D airspace, clear of all obstacles, and right for a magnetic course of 0° to 179° [[1:407|PHAK 16-20]].

callout.text: Altitude choice is more than clearance. Also consider cloud heights, winds, terrain and radio reception [[1:422|PHAK 16-35]]. Higher altitude improves radio and radar range [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]].

check.q: Your magnetic course is 210° and you will cruise well above 3,000 ft AGL. Pick: 5,500 or 6,500 ft MSL?
check.a: 6,500. Courses 180° to 359° use even thousands + 500 [[60:468|14 CFR 91.159(a)(2)]].

body.p: Wind moves the whole air mass, and you with it. Heading is where the nose points. Track is your path over the ground. The angle between them is drift [[1:396|PHAK 16-9]]. Point the nose into the wind by the wind correction angle so track matches course [[1:396|PHAK 16-9]].

Wind triangle example: TC 090°, wind from 045° at 40 knots, TAS 120 knots. Result: WCA 14° left, TH 076°, GS 88 knots [[1:402|PHAK 16-15]]. Draw the wind arrow downwind, the way the wind blows [[1:402|PHAK 16-15]].

head: Find
Formula
PHAK example
rows: 220 NM ÷ 88 kt = 2.5 hr; × 8 GPH = about 20 gal [[1:402|PHAK 16-15]]

bullets: Minutes to hours: divide by 60. 30 min = 0.5 hr [[1:398|PHAK 16-11]].
Knots to mph: multiply by 1.15. 20 knots = 23 mph [[1:398|PHAK 16-11]].
With wind, use GS (not TAS) for time and fuel [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].
Add fuel for start, taxi and climb. Climb GS is lower than cruise GS [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].

callout.text: 14 CFR 91.151: in an airplane under VFR you need fuel to reach your first landing point plus 30 minutes by day, or 45 minutes at night, at normal cruise [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151]].

check.q: Wind is from your right. Do you add or subtract the WCA from the true course?
check.a: Add it. Wind from the right: add; from the left: subtract [[1:403|PHAK 16-16]].

chunks.title: True airspeed, density altitude and power setting

body.p: True airspeed (TAS) is calibrated airspeed corrected for altitude and nonstandard temperature. It is the speed used for flight planning and on the flight plan [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]]. For the same calibrated airspeed, TAS goes up as altitude goes up [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]].

bullets: Best way: flight computer with CAS, pressure altitude and temperature [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]].
Rule of thumb: add 2% to CAS for each 1,000 ft [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]].
Density altitude is pressure altitude corrected for nonstandard temperature. High density altitude means less power, thrust and lift [[1:91|PHAK 4-4]].

body.p: **Power setting.** Pick a cruise power from the POH cruise chart. It gives rpm, percent power, TAS and fuel burn for your altitude [[1:280|PHAK 11-24]]. Sample chart: 5,000 ft at 2,400 rpm gives 116 mph TAS and 6.9 GPH; maximum cruise is normally limited to 75% power [[1:280|PHAK 11-24]].

Fuel burn depends on engine condition, propeller pitch and rpm, mixture, and the percent of horsepower used [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]]. As you climb, the mixture gets richer, so lean it with the mixture control as the POH says [[1:169|PHAK 7-9]].

callout.text: Higher power = faster but more gallons per hour. Use the same power setting in flight that you planned with, or your times and fuel numbers will not match.

check.q: Indicated (calibrated) airspeed is 110 knots at 5,000 ft. Rough TAS?
check.a: About 121 knots: add 2% per 1,000 ft, so 10% [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]].

chunks.title: Fly it step by step: plan, log and fly the leg

body.p: **On the ground** (PHAK sequence [[1:405|PHAK 16-18]]):

bullets: 1. Check weather and gather a current sectional, plotter and flight computer [[1:404|PHAK 16-17]].
2. Draw the course, choose checkpoints, and check airspace, terrain and obstacles [[1:405|PHAK 16-18]].
3. Choose a cruising altitude. Measure total distance and leg distances, and the TC [[1:407|PHAK 16-20]].
4. Work TC ± WCA = TH ± V = MH ± D = CH, then GS, leg times and fuel [[1:407|PHAK 16-20]].
5. Fill in the flight log. Add time for the climb (PHAK used 5 min) [[1:408|PHAK 16-21]].

body.p: **In the air:**

bullets: 6. Set the heading indicator to the compass in straight-and-level flight [[1:224|PHAK 8-22]]. Turn onto the compass heading over your departure point and write down the time [[1:408|PHAK 16-21]].
7. Hold heading and altitude. Your GS sets the time you should reach each checkpoint, so look for it at its ETA [[1:400|PHAK 16-13]].

8. At each checkpoint, write the actual time. GS = distance between two points ÷ time [[1:396|PHAK 16-9]]. Adjust heading, GS and time, then give a new ETA for the next checkpoint and the destination [[1:408|PHAK 16-21]].
9. If you drift, fix it by changing heading toward the course, using pilotage to confirm [[1:400|PHAK 16-13]].
10. If one checkpoint is missed, hold your heading and look for the next one [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].

head: ACS standard
Tolerance
rows: Within 3 NM of the planned route (ACS PA.VI.A.S5)
Within 5 minutes of the initial or revised ETA, and give a destination estimate (ACS PA.VI.A.S6)

callout.text: 3 NM is a little less than half an inch on a sectional (half an inch = 3.43 NM) [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]]. Use your brackets: if you would cross the bracket road or river, you are off course.

check.q: You planned 6 minutes for a 10 NM leg but it took 8. What is your actual GS and what do you do?
check.a: 10 NM ÷ (8/60) hr = 75 knots. Use the new GS to revise the ETA for the next checkpoint and the destination, and check fuel [[1:396|PHAK 16-9]] [[1:408|PHAK 16-21]].

chunks.title: Risk: traffic, distraction, getting lost and fuel

body.p: **Collision hazards.** Navigation pulls your eyes inside. It takes 1 to 2 seconds to refocus from the panel to something a mile away [[16:5|AC 90-48E 8.1.4]], and about 12.5 seconds to see, decide and move the airplane out of the way [[16:6|AC 90-48E Table 1]]. An airplane on a collision course seems to sit still, then suddenly fills the window [[16:6|AC 90-48E 8.1.8]].

bullets: Keep chart work short and look outside between steps. Fixation on displays draws attention away from traffic [[16:14|AC 90-48E 15]].
In cruise, make gentle shallow banks left and right to clear blind spots [[16:13|AC 90-48E 12.1]].
Be extra watchful near VFR waypoints, VORs and NDBs, where traffic gathers. Monitor ATC and use landing lights [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]].
Haze hides traffic. Flying above a haze layer helps [[16:7|AC 90-48E 8.1.9]].

body.p: **Distraction and lost awareness.** Fatigue, stress and work overload make you fixate on one item [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. Plan ahead: review the chart and set radios early, in low-workload times [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. A passenger can hold the chart [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]]. When overloaded: stop, think, slow down, prioritize [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].

head: If you are lost
Why
rows: Hold the heading. Turning away makes it easy to get more lost [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]]
Keeps your dead reckoning picture valid
Better radio, nav and radar range
Use VOR, GPS, or a town name on a water tower [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]]
ATC can give vectors to a landing site

body.p: **Unplanned fuel use.** Stronger headwinds, a richer mixture or a higher power setting burn more than planned. Land before your flight time exceeds the time your fuel was planned for, or before the gauge shows low fuel [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]]. Operating without adequate reserves comes from overconfidence or poor planning [[1:61|PHAK 2-22]].

callout.text: Diverting? In an emergency, turn toward the alternate first; do the math after. Then note the time and figure new heading, GS, ETA and fuel [[1:422|PHAK 16-35]].

check.q: You can't find your checkpoint and feel unsure. What is the first thing NOT to do?
check.a: Don't turn away from your heading. If confused, hold the heading [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].

bullets: Measuring the course at the departure point instead of a meridian near the middle [[1:392|PHAK 16-5]].
Applying variation the wrong way. West add, east subtract [[1:395|PHAK 16-8]].
Drawing the wind arrow toward where the wind comes from instead of downwind [[1:402|PHAK 16-15]].
Using TAS instead of GS for time and fuel when there is wind [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].
Forgetting climb time and fuel [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].
Picking small-circle towns or a single checkpoint with no backup [[1:405|PHAK 16-18]] [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].
Not resetting the heading indicator to the compass [[1:224|PHAK 8-22]].
Reading the compass during turns or speed changes [[1:228|PHAK 8-26]].
Turning around to look for a missed checkpoint instead of holding heading [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].
Heads-down navigation with no outside scan [[16:14|AC 90-48E 15]].

check.q: Why measure the true course at a meridian near the middle of the line?
check.a: Meridians converge toward the poles, so the midpoint gives the most accurate course [[1:392|PHAK 16-5]].

scenario.title: Haze, a stronger headwind and a missed checkpoint
scenario.setup: You are flying a 90 NM solo cross-country at 5,500 ft. Visibility is 6 SM in haze. You planned 100 knots GS and have 3.5 hours of fuel at your planned power. At checkpoint 2 you are 6 minutes late, and you can't spot checkpoint 3, a small town. You start digging through the chart and fiddling with the GPS.

questions.q: What is the biggest immediate risk while you look down at the chart and GPS?
questions.a: A midair collision. In haze, traffic is hard to see [[16:7|AC 90-48E 8.1.9]], and it takes about 12.5 seconds to see and avoid [[16:6|AC 90-48E Table 1]]. Keep head-down work short and keep scanning [[16:14|AC 90-48E 15]].

questions.q: You can't find checkpoint 3. What do you do first?
questions.a: Hold your heading and look for the next checkpoint [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]]. If still unsure, climb (watching traffic and weather), use VOR or GPS for a fix, and talk to ATC [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]].

questions.q: Being 6 minutes late at checkpoint 2 tells you what about the wind and fuel?
questions.a: The headwind is stronger than forecast, so GS is lower. Compute the actual GS from distance and time [[1:396|PHAK 16-9]], revise the ETA and fuel, and be ready to land before your flight time passes your fuel time [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].

questions.q: Suppose the headwind keeps building and your revised fuel at the destination comes out under 30 minutes. What now?
questions.a: Divert or land early. 14 CFR 91.151 requires at least 30 minutes of fuel after the first point of intended landing (daytime VFR) when you begin a flight [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151]]; don't plan to land with less. Turn toward a nearer airport, then figure heading, GS, ETA and fuel [[1:422|PHAK 16-35]].

skills.do: Show a completed flight log (courses, checkpoints, distances, headings, GS, times, fuel) and fill in actual times in flight.
skills.practice: Plan the PHAK Chickasha-to-Guthrie trip yourself and compare with Figure 16-26 [[1:407|PHAK 16-20]]. Then plan your own local route.

skills.do: Find and name checkpoints by matching the ground to the chart.
skills.practice: Fly a planned leg with the GPS covered. Call out each checkpoint and the brackets on either side [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].

skills.do: Fly pre-computed compass headings and use elapsed time to know where you are.
skills.practice: Start the timer over each checkpoint. At the ETA, look for the next one. Compute actual GS between checkpoints [[1:396|PHAK 16-9]].

skills.do: Use the compass and heading indicator, including turns to headings.
skills.practice: Reset the heading indicator to the compass about every 15 minutes [[1:224|PHAK 8-22]]. Practice compass-only turns to north and south using the lead/lag rule [[1:228|PHAK 8-26]].

skills.do: Stay within 3 NM of the planned route (ACS PA.VI.A.S5).
skills.practice: Pick brackets on both sides of the course and correct heading as soon as you see drift [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].

skills.do: Arrive at checkpoints within 5 minutes of the initial or revised ETA and give a destination estimate (ACS PA.VI.A.S6).
skills.practice: At each checkpoint, say out loud the new GS, next ETA and destination ETA [[1:408|PHAK 16-21]].

skills.do: Hold the chosen altitude ±200 ft and heading ±15° (ACS PA.VI.A.S7).
skills.practice: Trim for cruise before doing any chart or log work, and glance at altitude and heading between each task.

quiz.q: Navigation by reference to visible landmarks is called:
quiz.why: Pilotage uses visible landmarks; dead reckoning uses computation [[1:388|PHAK 16-1]].

quiz.q: TC 031°, WCA 3° L, variation 7° E, deviation +2°. Compass heading?
On a westerly heading you slow down. The magnetic compass will show:
quiz.why: ANDS: deceleration shows a turn toward south on east or west headings [[1:228|PHAK 8-26]].

quiz.q: Near 40° latitude, using the PHAK rule, when do you stop a turn to north on the magnetic compass?
quiz.why: 15° + half the latitude (20°) = 35°, stopped before the heading [[1:228|PHAK 8-26]].

quiz.q: A Maximum Elevation Figure of "45" on a sectional means:
options: Highest terrain or obstacle in the quadrant is 4,500 ft MSL or less
The highest tower is 450 ft AGL
quiz.why: The MEF is the highest elevation in the quadrant, rounded up to the next 100 ft, last two digits not shown [[2:12|Chart Users' Guide p 12]].

quiz.q: Magnetic course 140°, more than 3,000 ft AGL, below 18,000 ft. Which VFR cruising altitude fits?
You fly 30 NM between checkpoints in 15 minutes. Your groundspeed is:
You're unsure of your position and can't find the next checkpoint. Best first action?
options: Turn around to find the last checkpoint
Hold heading, then climb and use radios or ATC if needed
Circle until you see a town
quiz.why: If confused, hold the heading [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]]. Climbing increases radio, navigation and radar range [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]].

takeaways: Use dead reckoning for heading and time, and pilotage to check them at each checkpoint.
TC ± WCA = TH ± V = MH ± D = CH. West add, east subtract.
Compass: ANDS; to north stop early, to south go past. Reset the heading indicator about every 15 minutes.
Pick big checkpoints with brackets, and an altitude that clears terrain, obstacles and follows 91.159.
At every checkpoint: actual time, new GS, new ETA, new fuel.
Lost? Hold heading, climb, communicate. Short on fuel? Divert early.
cfi_notes: Have students plan the PHAK Chickasha-to-Guthrie trip and compare to Figure 16-26 before they plan their own.
Figure 16-26 lists 8,000 ft on the planning sheet and log, but the PHAK text chose 5,500 ft (16-20 and the flight plan in Figure 16-27). Point this out so students don't copy it.
Examiners commonly ask for a revised ETA after the first checkpoint and a destination estimate. Have students say it out loud on every training cross-country.
Common mistake: drawing the wind vector toward 045° instead of downwind. Have them say 'wind FROM, arrow points TO'.
PHAK uses '15° plus half the latitude' for compass lead/lag; the IFH uses 'latitude plus/minus half the bank' [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]. Teach one and know the other exists.
Train with the GPS covered. Then show how GPS can back up, not replace, pilotage [[1:409|PHAK 16-22]].
gaps: The AFH has no pilotage/dead-reckoning procedure or common-errors list; the step-by-step and common errors come from PHAK Ch 16 and AC 90-48E.
No source gives an off-course correction rule of thumb (e.g. 1-in-60) for regaining the course; students learn heading correction by practice.
Cruise power settings, fuel burn and TAS for the training airplane come from its POH; the PHAK chart numbers are only a sample.
Exact current isogonic values and MEFs must come from the current sectional, not this lesson.

activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.

items.t: Wind blows from the right of your course (WCA)
Wind blows from the left of your course (WCA)
Deviation card shows +3° for your heading
Deviation card shows -2° for your heading

activities.title: Outsmart the compass
activities.intro: Tap a situation, then what the compass does or what you should do.

pairs.r: Card leads, so roll out before the heading
Card lags, so let it pass the heading first

pairs.l: Speeding up, heading east or west
pairs.r: Shows a false turn toward north

pairs.l: Slowing down, heading east or west
pairs.r: Shows a false turn toward south
Use the average of the swings
Readings are erratic and can't be trusted

activities.title: True or false: chart, route and wind

cards.s: On a sectional, contour lines that are close together show a steep slope.
cards.why: Yes. Close lines mean steep slopes; widely spaced lines mean gentle slopes [[2:10|Chart Users' Guide p 10]].

cards.s: On an obstruction label, the number in parentheses is the height of the top above sea level (MSL).
cards.why: No. The top is shown in MSL. The number in parentheses is the height above the ground (AGL) [[2:11|Chart Users' Guide p 11]].

cards.s: Towns shown as a small circle are usually the best checkpoints.
cards.why: No. A small-circle town may be only a half-dozen houses. Choose towns shown by splashes of yellow [[1:405|PHAK 16-18]].

cards.s: When there is a headwind, use groundspeed, not true airspeed, to figure time and fuel.
cards.why: Yes. GS sets the time the flight takes, so you must use GS to calculate fuel when wind is present [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].

cards.s: On a wind triangle, draw the wind arrow pointing toward the direction the wind comes from.
cards.why: No. Draw it downwind, the way the wind is blowing [[1:402|PHAK 16-15]].

cards.s: For a day VFR flight in an airplane, you need fuel to reach your first point of intended landing plus 30 more minutes at normal cruise.
cards.why: Yes. At night it is 45 minutes [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151(a)]].

activities.title: From chart to compass heading
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Check the weather: is the flight possible, and which route is best?
Draw the course line from airport center to airport center
Measure the true course at a meridian near the middle
Apply the wind correction angle to get true heading
Apply variation to get magnetic heading
Apply deviation to get compass heading
In flight, note the time at each checkpoint and figure the actual GS

final_quiz.q: On a typical cross-country over land, how do dead reckoning and pilotage work together?
options: You pick one method before takeoff and use only that one
Pilotage gives you the heading, and dead reckoning is only for emergencies
Dead reckoning gives a heading and GS, and pilotage checks them at each checkpoint
Dead reckoning is only used after the GPS fails
final_quiz.why: Except over water, dead reckoning is usually used with pilotage. The computed heading and GS are watched and corrected by pilotage at checkpoints [[1:400|PHAK 16-13]].

final_quiz.q: TC 245°. Wind is from the right, WCA 6°. Variation is 4° W. The deviation card shows -2° for this heading. What compass heading do you fly?
final_quiz.why: Wind from the right: add, 245 + 6 = 251° TH. West variation: add, 251 + 4 = 255° MH. Deviation -2: 253° CH [[1:403|PHAK 16-16]] [[1:395|PHAK 16-8]].

final_quiz.q: Near 34° N latitude you turn right from east to south using only the magnetic compass. By the PHAK rule, when should you roll out?
final_quiz.why: Turning to south, the card lags, so let it pass the heading by 15° plus half the latitude: 15 + 17 = 32°, so roll out near 212° [[1:228|PHAK 8-26]].

final_quiz.q: In one sectional quadrant, the highest point is a tower whose top is 3,420 ft MSL, well above the terrain. What Maximum Elevation Figure will the chart show?
final_quiz.why: Add 100 ft for possible error (3,520 ft), then round up to the next 100 ft: 3,600 ft, printed as "36" [[2:12|Chart Users' Guide p 12]].

final_quiz.q: A tower on your route is labeled 1549 with (412) under it. PHAK says never approach antennas less than 500 ft above the tallest one. What is the lowest altitude for passing over it?
final_quiz.why: 1549 is the top in MSL; (412) is its height AGL [[2:11|Chart Users' Guide p 11]]. 1,549 + 500 = 2,049 ft MSL [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].

final_quiz.q: Your true course is 174°. Variation is 9° W. You will cruise more than 3,000 ft above the ground, below 18,000 ft. Which altitude is correct?
final_quiz.why: West variation is added: magnetic course 183° [[1:395|PHAK 16-8]]. Courses of 180° to 359° use even thousands + 500, so 4,500 ft [[60:468|14 CFR 91.159(a)(2)]].

final_quiz.q: Your TAS is 125 knots, but a headwind gives a GS of 112 knots. The leg is 84 NM and you burn 9 GPH. About how much fuel does the leg use?
final_quiz.why: Time = 84 ÷ 112 = 0.75 hr (45 min). Fuel = 0.75 × 9 = 6.75 gallons [[1:398|PHAK 16-11]]. With wind you must use GS, not TAS [[1:399|PHAK 16-12]].

final_quiz.q: A night VFR flight will take 1 hour 40 minutes at normal cruise, burning 8 GPH. Ignoring taxi and climb, what is the least fuel you may start with?
final_quiz.why: At night you need fuel to the first landing point plus 45 minutes [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151(a)(2)]]. 1:40 + 0:45 = 2:25, about 2.42 hr × 8 = about 19.3 gallons. 17.3 uses the 30-minute day reserve.

final_quiz.q: You plan to cruise at 6,000 ft with a calibrated airspeed of 105 knots. Using the rule of thumb, what TAS do you put on your plan?
final_quiz.why: Add 2% of CAS per 1,000 ft: 6 × 2% = 12%, and 105 × 1.12 = about 118 knots [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]].

final_quiz.q: You planned 108 knots GS. Two checkpoints 18 NM apart take you 12 minutes. 54 NM remain to the destination. What is your new time en route from here?
final_quiz.why: Actual GS = 18 NM ÷ 0.2 hr = 90 knots [[1:396|PHAK 16-9]]. Time = 54 ÷ 90 = 0.6 hr = 36 minutes [[1:398|PHAK 16-11]]. 30 minutes is the old plan.

final_quiz.q: According to AC 90-48E, about how long does it take from first seeing traffic until your airplane actually starts to move away?
final_quiz.why: Recognizing, deciding, reacting and aircraft lag add up to about 12.5 seconds [[16:6|AC 90-48E Table 1]]. That is why long head-down chart work is risky.

final_quiz.q: In an emergency you must divert to an alternate airport. What does the PHAK say to do?
options: Turn toward the alternate right away, then note the time and figure heading, GS, ETA and fuel
Plot the new course and finish all the math before turning
Keep going to your destination and do the math after landing
Circle in place until you have plotted the new route
final_quiz.why: In an emergency, divert promptly. Doing all the plotting first may make the emergency worse. Once on course, note the time and compute heading, GS, arrival time and fuel [[1:422|PHAK 16-35]].
